headline: Ancient Freediving Skills Help Indonesia's Bajau Reclaim Sea Heritage
meta_description: Indonesia's Bajau people are reviving traditional freediving practices, preserving centuries-old skills while protecting marine life and their own health.
summary_short: A ban on dangerous compressor diving in Indonesia is helping the Bajau people return to traditional freediving—a safer, more sustainable way to fish.
body:
When Mahari surveys the waters off Poto Tano on Sumbawa island, he's practicing a skill his people have refined across generations. The Bajau are an Indigenous ethnic group spanning Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, traditionally living on boats and harvesting from the sea through freediving. Now, a recent ban on compressor-assisted diving in West Nusa Tenggara province is giving these time-honored techniques new purpose. Mahari and around 40 other octopus fishermen have joined PELITA, a community-based fishery group partnering with the Jari Foundation and local government, trading the dangerous pull of compressor diving for the precision of traditional methods—and discovering that old ways often work best.

The shift represents more than nostalgia. Compressor diving, where divers breathe surface air pumped through long hoses, carries severe risks: decompression sickness, paralysis, chronic disabilities, and drowning. Freediving, while having minor pressure-related hazards, is gentler on both body and marine ecosystems. Using tools like the pocong—a wooden decoy resembling an octopus—skilled fishers like Nadir dive to 15–20 meters and lure their catch by hand. "Only 10 people in their community can use the pocong," one fisher explains. "You need strength and skill." It takes a lifetime to master.

What makes this revival remarkable is how it reconnects younger generations to heritage while addressing immediate hardship. Many Bajau felt economic pressure to adopt compressor diving, needing larger catches to support families. Through PELITA, named after the traditional oil lamps that once lit fishing villages, the community is finding that returning to freediving—paired with marine conservation work and ecotourism—can sustain livelihoods without sacrificing health or the sea itself. As one fisher, Well, acknowledged: "With compressor diving, you get more money. There's temptation." But recognizing the costs, these fishermen are choosing differently, proving that cultural knowledge and ecological responsibility can be the same choice.
quick_facts: Bajau people of Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines traditionally fish using freediving
Recent compressor diving ban in West Nusa Tenggara province now protects fishers
PELITA group includes ~40 octopus fishermen returning to traditional methods
Pocong fishing technique requires divers to reach 15–20 meters depth
